source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"It mechanically restrains the client in bed and therefore replaces all other individualized fall interventions","B":"It alerts staff to movement or attempted bed exit but does not physically prevent the client from leaving","C":"It locks the bed rails in place and prevents voluntary movement until a nurse deactivates the device","D":"It eliminates fall risk once activated, so reassessment and a tailored prevention plan are unnecessary"}}
source_row.rationale: Bed-exit alarms are monitoring/alert tools, not physical barriers. Fall prevention should be individualized and layered; an alarm does not replace risk assessment, assistance, toileting plans, environmental measures, or other indicated interventions.
source_row.source_detail: AHRQ PSNet describes bed alarms as devices used to notify staff when a patient attempts to get out of bed; they are an alerting intervention rather than a device that physically confines the patient.
source_row.stem: A family member asks whether a bed-exit alarm physically keeps a high-risk client in bed. Which response is most accurate?
